Overview Water resources include rivers, lakes, groundwater, reservoirs, wetlands, and reused water. A watershed is the land area that drains to a common outlet. Activities upstream can affect water quantity and quality downstream, so water management often requires coordination across communities and jurisdictions. Key principles Groundwater is stored in pores and fractures underground. Aquifers recharge at different rates; pumping faster than replenishment can lower water levels, increase pumping costs, affect connected streams, or contribute to land subsidence. Water budgets compare supply, demand, storage, and losses over time. Practical steps Conservation measures include repairing leaks, choosing efficient fixtures, matching outdoor irrigation to plant needs, using mulch, and selecting climate-appropriate landscaping. Large users can audit processes, meter consumption, and reuse suitable water where regulations and health safeguards allow. excerpt: Data Literacy | Everything Hub Everything Hub / Data Literacy Data Literacy Read charts, evaluate statistics, understand uncertainty, and avoid misleading conclusions. Overview Data literacy is the ability to interpret, question, and communicate information derived from data. Begin by asking who collected the data, how variables were defined, what population was measured, when collection occurred, and what was excluded. Key principles A count and a rate answer different questions. A percentage needs a denominator. Averages can be distorted by extreme values, while medians describe the midpoint. Always inspect units, time periods, sample sizes, and missing data before comparing figures. Practical steps Correlation means two variables move together; it does not by itself establish that one caused the other. Confounding variables, selection effects, measurement error, and small samples can produce misleading patterns. Look for study design and plausible alternative explanations. A hypothesis should make predictions that evidence could support or contradict. Scientific conclusions remain open to refinement when better data or methods become available. Key principles A good study defines variables, sampling methods, procedures, and analysis before interpreting results. Controls help isolate the factor being tested. Practical steps Peer review is a quality-control step, not a guarantee that a finding is correct.
